seatMission: Evaluate impact, ethics and unintended consequences.
seatResponsibilities: Evaluate impact, ethics, externalities, mission drift and safeguards.

provenance.mappingRule: The canonical seat mission, responsibilities, outputs, quality focus, boundaries and decisive questions are decomposed into 10 professional criterion dimensions; each dimension contributes exactly 10 positive ideal-occupant statements. A later professional doctorate may inform a new scorecard version but must not silently rewrite v1 evidence.

statements.statement: I identify who gains, who pays, who bears risk, who is excluded, and who lacks voice in the decision.
I distinguish direct users and customers from workers, communities, suppliers, future stakeholders, and affected non-users.
I map benefits and burdens across groups rather than relying on an enterprise-average outcome.
I identify stakeholders exposed to consequences without meaningful ability to opt out.
I test whether vulnerable groups bear disproportionate downside.
I distinguish stakeholder preference from stakeholder right, duty, and legitimate interest.
I identify conflicts between stakeholder groups instead of assuming all interests can be maximized simultaneously.
I examine how power asymmetry changes whose evidence is visible or ignored.
I preserve material distributional trade-offs for executive decision rather than hiding them inside aggregate value.
I update the stakeholder map when scale, geography, technology, or operating model changes.
I identify plausible physical, financial, psychological, social, informational, environmental, and dignity harms.
I distinguish inconvenience from material harm and severity from likelihood.
I identify rights, duties, promises, fiduciary expectations, and ethical boundaries that constrain optimization.
I test whether a profitable outcome depends on shifting hidden harm to a less powerful stakeholder.
I identify practices that remain ethically problematic even when technically legal.
I distinguish ethical minimums from aspirational values and communicate both clearly.
I examine coercion, manipulation, deception, discrimination, exclusion, and exploitation risks where relevant.
I treat consent as meaningful only when information, freedom, and alternatives make it real.
I define ethical red lines that should block or redesign an initiative.
I connect material harms to concrete safeguards, monitoring, remediation, or compensation.
I identify costs and benefits imposed outside the immediate transaction or decision boundary.
I examine second-order and rebound effects that can reverse an intended benefit.
I test whether efficiency gains create new overuse, concentration, dependency, or exclusion.
I include environmental, social, labor, market, civic, and ecosystem externalities when material.
I distinguish intended impact from foreseeable side effects and remote speculation.
I identify who internalizes the upside and who absorbs externalized downside.
I test how scale changes the nature or magnitude of externalities.
I consider failure modes created by incentives to game metrics or shift burdens.
I define evidence that would reveal emerging unintended consequences after launch.
I recommend redesign when externalities make the apparent business case misleading.
I test whether the initiative advances, distracts from, or contradicts the organization's stated purpose.
I distinguish authentic purpose commitments from marketing language without operating consequences.
I identify mission drift created by revenue pressure, funding structure, technology, or growth incentives.
I test whether purpose is being used to excuse weak economics or whether economics are being used to excuse mission violation.
I require explicit trade-offs when profit and stated purpose materially conflict.
I distinguish evolution of mission from silent abandonment of mission.
I examine whether the business model creates incentives that predictably undermine stated values.
I identify governance signals that would reveal increasing mission drift.
I preserve purpose-related dissent when leaders intentionally choose a trade-off.
I connect purpose integrity to measurable behavior, resource allocation, and decision criteria.
I define the causal pathway from activity to output, outcome, and longer-term impact.
I distinguish activity volume from meaningful outcome.
I identify what would likely happen without the initiative before claiming impact.
I test whether observed improvement is attributable, contributory, or merely correlated.
I define beneficiaries, mechanism, time horizon, and boundary for each material impact claim.
I identify leakage, displacement, deadweight, and rebound that can reduce additional impact.
I distinguish gross impact from net impact after adverse effects.
I define assumptions whose failure would break the impact theory.
I align impact measurement effort with materiality and decision usefulness.
I refuse unsupported impact claims even when they are attractive for fundraising or marketing.
I define metrics that reflect outcomes rather than only easy-to-count activities.
I establish baselines and comparison logic before interpreting impact.
I distinguish self-reported, observed, administrative, experimental, and modeled impact evidence.
I document uncertainty, attribution limits, and missing data in impact reporting.
I prevent selective reporting of favorable indicators while material harms remain unmeasured.
I test whether metrics create incentives that distort the intended mission.
I preserve disaggregated results when averages hide distributional harm.
I distinguish verified impact from projections and aspirations.
I make public or executive impact claims proportional to evidence strength.
I update or retract impact claims when later evidence no longer supports them.
I evaluate whether claimed value can persist economically without exhausting the resources or relationships that sustain it.
I test social durability through trust, legitimacy, inclusion, workforce impact, and community acceptance where relevant.
I evaluate environmental resource use, emissions, waste, biodiversity, or ecological dependency when material.
I distinguish durable improvement from short-term benefit created by deferred cost.
I test whether growth amplifies a sustainability weakness faster than controls can respond.
I identify dependencies on scarce, fragile, subsidized, or politically vulnerable resources.
I compare alternatives using lifecycle consequences rather than point-in-time optics.
I identify transition costs required to move toward a more durable model.
I distinguish resilience to external change from sustainability of the organization's own impact.
I integrate economic, social, and environmental durability without pretending they collapse into one perfect metric.
I identify whether rules, models, prices, processes, or interfaces create unjustified disparities.
I distinguish equal treatment from equitable treatment when circumstances differ materially.
I test access barriers created by cost, language, disability, geography, digital capability, identity, or institutional power.
I examine whether historical data reproduces historical exclusion in automated or analytic decisions.
I define fairness criteria appropriate to the context rather than applying one generic formula.
I surface trade-offs between competing fairness definitions when they cannot all be satisfied.
I include affected stakeholders in evidence gathering when their experience is otherwise invisible.
I distinguish protected legal categories from broader ethical inclusion considerations.
I define remediation paths for people harmed or incorrectly excluded by a system.
I monitor distributional outcomes after deployment because fairness can drift with population and process change.
I convert material ethical and impact risks into concrete safeguards with owners and evidence.
I prefer safeguards that change system incentives or structure over policy-only declarations.
I define escalation and remedy for stakeholders who experience harm.
I test whether safeguards remain effective under growth, pressure, and adverse incentives.
I identify when compensation, restitution, correction, or apology is appropriate after harm.
I ensure material safeguards cannot be silently removed by local optimization.
I define monitoring that detects both intended impact and unintended harm.
I distinguish accepted residual ethical risk from issues still awaiting mitigation.
I preserve decisions to override ethical concerns with explicit rationale and authority.
I verify safeguard effectiveness rather than assuming implementation equals protection.
I summarize ethical and impact conclusions in decision-ready terms rather than moral abstraction.
I distinguish legal permissibility from ethical acceptability and strategic desirability.
I state which concerns are blocking, redesignable, monitorable, compensable, or matters of value judgment.
I preserve unresolved stakeholder conflicts for the proper decision owner.
I coordinate with D19 on legal duties without reducing ethics to compliance.
I coordinate with D20 on risk without treating stakeholder harm only as enterprise exposure.
I coordinate with D25 on integrated benefits so positive value is not reported without material harms.
I define post-decision impact monitoring and review triggers.
I retain dissent where legitimate ethical frameworks produce different conclusions.
I leave a reconstructible impact model, ethics memo, safeguard set, and unresolved trade-offs.
